lehigh-2003-04.title: Compare the gaps from 1
lehigh-2003-04.body:
Each fraction equals $1$ minus a small fraction: $a=1-\frac4{15}$, $b=1-\frac6{19}$, $c=1-\frac7{23}$.

Compare $\frac4{15}\approx0.267$, $\frac6{19}\approx0.316$, $\frac7{23}\approx0.304$. The larger the gap, the smaller the number, so $b<c<a$.

(Decimals: $a\approx0.733$, $b\approx0.684$, $c\approx0.696$.)

**Answer: $b,c,a$**

lehigh-2003-05.title: Roots of each factor
lehigh-2003-05.body:
$y=0$ iff some factor is $0$. The discriminants $b^2-4ac$ of the three quadratics are $25-36=-11$, $36-36=0$, and $49-36=13$: respectively $0$, $1$, and $2$ real roots.

The roots are distinct ($x=3$ is not a root of the third factor, since $9-21+9\neq0$), so there are $0+1+2=3$ intersection points.

**Answer: 3**

lehigh-2003-06.title: Subtract
lehigh-2003-06.body:
Subtracting the equations gives $y^2-y=2$, so $(y-2)(y+1)=0$ and $y=2$ or $y=-1$. Each gives a unique $x$ ($x=0$ or $x=3$).

**Answer: 2**

lehigh-2003-07.title: Count the multiples
lehigh-2003-07.body:
The smallest multiple of $7$ above $100$ is $105=7\cdot15$ and the largest below $1000$ is $994=7\cdot142$. That is $142-15+1=128$ multiples.

**Answer: 128**

lehigh-2003-08.title: An annulus
lehigh-2003-08.body:
The parasol's center moves on a circle of radius $6$ and the parasol has radius $2$, so the dead grass is the ring of points at distance between $6-2=4$ and $6+2=8$ from the center of the lawn circle.

Area: $\pi(8^2-4^2)=48\pi$ square feet.

**Answer: $48\pi$**

lehigh-2003-09.title: Pythagoras
lehigh-2003-09.body:
Let the other leg be $x$; the hypotenuse is $x+2$. Then $(x+2)^2=x^2+5^2$, so $4x+4=25$ and $x=\frac{21}4$. The hypotenuse is $\frac{29}4$.

Perimeter: $5+\frac{21}4+\frac{29}4=\frac{35}{2}=17\frac12$.

**Answer: $17\frac12$**

lehigh-2003-10.title: Chain of implications
lehigh-2003-10.body:
Since $y=0$: by (a) (contrapositive) $x=1$. By (b), $w=z$. If $z=0$, then $w=z=0$, but (c) would require $w=1$, a contradiction. So $z=1$ and $w=1$.

$w+x+z=1+1+1=3$.

**Answer: 3**

lehigh-2003-11.title: Find the purchase prices
lehigh-2003-11.body:
First car: $1.4x=840$, so the dealer paid $x=600$. Second car: $0.75y=840$, so he paid $y=1120$.

He paid $600+1120=1720$ and received $2\cdot840=1680$, a net **loss of $\$40$**.

**Answer: a loss of $\$40$**

lehigh-2003-12.title: Pigeonhole principle
lehigh-2003-12.body:
The worst case is picking $6$ of each color that has at least $6$ balls (green, red, blue, yellow, black) and all $4$ white balls, with no color having $7$: $5\cdot6+4=34$ balls.

The next ball must give $7$ of some color. So $35$ balls are needed.

**Answer: 35**

lehigh-2003-13.title: Speeds
lehigh-2003-13.body:
Let $s_B,s_M$ be the speeds and $d$ the distance. Then $5s_B+5s_M=d$. In the second scenario Bill walks $3$ minutes and Mary $6$ minutes: $3s_B+6s_M=d$.

Equating, $2s_B=s_M$. So $d=5s_B+10s_B=15s_B$, and Bill needs $15$ minutes.

**Answer: 15 minutes**

lehigh-2003-15.title: Differences
lehigh-2003-15.body: For a quadratic the first differences at equally spaced points increase linearly. $p(2)-p(1)=1$ and $p(3)-p(2)=2$, so the next differences are $3$ and $4$: $p(4)=7$ and $p(5)=11$.

lehigh-2003-16.title: Factor
lehigh-2003-16.body:
$|x^2-4|=|x+2|\cdot|x-2|$. For $-2.1<x<-1.9$, $|x+2|<0.1$ and $|x-2|$ is between $3.9$ and $4.1$.

The product is largest near the end $x=-2.1$, where it equals $0.1\cdot4.1=0.41$. As the inequality is strict, this value is approached but not attained: $0.41$ is the supremum (the intended condition was $|x+2|\le0.1$, with maximum $0.41$).

**Answer: $0.41$**

lehigh-2003-17.title: Gasoline equation
lehigh-2003-17.body:
Let $x$ be the city mpg. Then $\frac{112}{x+3}+\frac{150}{x}=10$, which simplifies to $5x^2-116x-225=0$, i.e. $(5x+9)(x-25)=0$. So $x=25$.

Check: $\frac{112}{28}+\frac{150}{25}=4+6=10$. ✓

**Answer: 25 mpg**

lehigh-2003-18.title: Similar triangles
lehigh-2003-18.body:
The triangle above the bottom line is similar to the whole with ratio $\frac56$, so its area is $\frac{25}{36}$ of the whole. The bottom part (the largest) therefore has area $\frac{11}{36}$ of the whole.

So the whole has area $33\cdot\frac{36}{11}=108$.

**Answer: 108**

lehigh-2003-19.title: Fractions of each class
lehigh-2003-19.body:
Let $s$ and $j$ be the fractions of seniors and juniors who said Yes (the classes have equal size). Seniors make up $70\%$ of the Yes answers: $\frac{s}{s+j}=\frac7{10}$, so $j=\frac37s$. Juniors make up $80\%$ of the No answers: $\frac{1-j}{(1-j)+(1-s)}=\frac45$, so $1-j=4(1-s)$.

Substituting: $1-\frac37s=4-4s$, so $\frac{25}7s=3$ and $s=\frac{21}{25}=84\%$.

**Answer: 84**

lehigh-2003-20.title: Substitute
lehigh-2003-20.body:
Let $y=2^{2^x}$. Then $4^{2^x}=(2^2)^{2^x}=(2^{2^x})^2=y^2$, so $y+y^2=56$, giving $y=7$ (positive root).

The desired quantity is $2^{2^{2^x}}=2^{y}=2^7=128$.

**Answer: 128**

lehigh-2003-21.title: Reduce to a common multiple
lehigh-2003-21.body:
The conditions say $k+3\mid n+k$ for $k=0,\dots,6$, i.e. $k+3\mid n-3$. So $n-3$ must be divisible by each of $3,4,\dots,9$, i.e. by $\mathrm{lcm}=8\cdot9\cdot5\cdot7=2520$.

The smallest is $n=3$, the next is $n=2523$.

**Answer: 2523**

lehigh-2003-22.title: Perpendicular diagonals
lehigh-2003-22.body:
Let the diagonals meet at $O$ and cut each other into segments $p,q$ (one diagonal) and $r,s$ (the other), so the sides in order satisfy $a^2=p^2+r^2$, $b^2=r^2+q^2$, $c^2=q^2+s^2$, $d^2=s^2+p^2$. Adding gives $a^2+c^2=b^2+d^2$: the sums of squares of opposite sides are equal.

With the sides $2,3,4$ and the unknown side $d$ opposite one of them: $d^2=2^2+3^2-4^2<0$ is impossible, $d^2=2^2+4^2-3^2=11$, or $d^2=3^2+4^2-2^2=21$. Both occur (any four lengths with equal sums of opposite squares form such a quadrilateral).

**Answer: $\sqrt{11}$ or $\sqrt{21}$**

lehigh-2003-23.title: Tangent addition
lehigh-2003-23.body:
Take the squares with side $1$. The slanting lines go from the top-left corner to the bottom corners at horizontal distance $2$ and $3$, so $\tan A=\frac12$ and $\tan B=\frac13$.

$$\tan(A+B)=\frac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac12\cdot\frac13}=\frac{5/6}{5/6}=1,$$
and $A+B$ is acute, so $A+B=\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi4$**

lehigh-2003-24.title: Isosceles triangle
lehigh-2003-24.body:
Triangle $OPQ$ is isosceles with $OP=OQ=8$ and apex angle $\frac{5\pi}{12}+\frac{3\pi}{12}=\frac{2\pi}3$. The midpoint $M$ of $PQ$ lies on the angle bisector, at angle $\frac12\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}-\frac{3\pi}{12}\right)=\frac{\pi}{12}$.

$OM=8\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=4$.

**Answer: $\left(4,\frac\pi{12}\right)$**

lehigh-2003-25.title: Sum a double series
lehigh-2003-25.body:
The circles are disjoint (radii at most $\frac16$), so we add areas: $\pi\sum_{m,n}\frac1{4^{|m|+1}9^{|n|+1}}=\pi\left(\sum_m\frac1{4^{|m|+1}}\right)\left(\sum_n\frac1{9^{|n|+1}}\right)$.

$\sum_m\frac1{4^{|m|+1}}=\frac14+2\cdot\frac{1/16}{1-1/4}=\frac14+\frac16=\frac5{12}$, and $\sum_n\frac1{9^{|n|+1}}=\frac19+2\cdot\frac{1/81}{1-1/9}=\frac19+\frac1{36}=\frac5{36}$.

Total: $\frac{5\pi}{12}\cdot\frac5{36}=\frac{25\pi}{432}$.

**Answer: $\frac{25\pi}{432}$**

lehigh-2003-26.title: Count by type
lehigh-2003-26.body:
Lines with lines: each vertical meets each horizontal once, $21\cdot21=441$ points (parallel lines do not meet; concentric circles do not meet).

The circle of radius $k+\frac1\pi$ meets $x=i$ in $2$ points when $|i|\le k$ (that is $2k+1$ lines, never tangent since the radius is not an integer), and the same for horizontals, for a total of $4(2k+1)$ points. Summing over $k=0,\dots,9$: $4(1+3+\cdots+19)=4\cdot100=400$.

Total: $441+400=841$.

**Answer: 841**

lehigh-2003-28.title: Work modulo 4
lehigh-2003-28.body:
$a_2=03=3$. The residue of $a^2$ modulo $8$ depends only on $a$ modulo $4$: $0\mapsto0$, $\pm1\mapsto1$, $2\mapsto4$.

Modulo $4$ the sequence is $0,3,3,2,1,3,0,3,\dots$, repeating with period $6$. The squares modulo $8$ over one period: $0+1+1+4+1+1=8\equiv0$.

$2003=6\cdot333+5$, so the sum is congruent to the first five terms of a period: $0+1+1+4+1=7$.

**Answer: 7**

lehigh-2003-29.title: Count backwards from the last letter

lehigh-2003-30.title: Sum positions
lehigh-2003-30.body:
Number the positions in the pile from the bottom: the bottom deck occupies $1,\dots,52$, the top deck $53,\dots,104$. If card $i$ has position $b_i$ in the bottom deck and $a_i$ in the top deck, the number of cards strictly between them is $a_i-b_i-1$.

Summing over all $52$ cards (each position used exactly once in each deck): $(53+\cdots+104)-(1+\cdots+52)-52=52\cdot52-52=2652$.

**Answer: 2652**

lehigh-2003-31.title: Exterior angles
lehigh-2003-31.body:
There are $n$ triangles built on the sides of the polygon, each with its apex at a point of the star. The base angles of these triangles are exactly the exterior angles of the polygon, taken at both ends of each side, i.e. each vertex of the polygon contributes two exterior angles (one from each adjacent triangle).

The exterior angles of a convex polygon sum to $360^\circ$ (one per vertex), so the total of all base angles is $2\cdot360^\circ=720^\circ$.

The $n$ triangles have angle sum $180n$, so the angles at the star's points sum to $180n-720=(n-4)\cdot180$ degrees. (For $n=5$: $180^\circ$ ✓.)

**Answer: $(n-4)180^\circ$**

lehigh-2003-32.title: Eliminate the legs
lehigh-2003-32.body:
Let the legs be $a,b$ and the hypotenuse $c$. Then $a^2+b^2=c^2$ and $Q=a^2+b^2+c^2=2c^2$, so $c=\sqrt{Q/2}$.

$P=a+b+c$, so $(a+b)^2=(P-c)^2$, giving $a^2+b^2+2ab=P^2-2Pc+c^2$. Since $a^2+b^2=c^2$: $2ab=P^2-2Pc$.

Area $=\frac{ab}2=\frac{P^2-2Pc}{4}=\frac14P^2-\frac12P\sqrt{\frac Q2}=\frac14P^2-\frac{\sqrt2}{4}P\sqrt Q$.

So $(k_1,k_2,k_3)=\left(\frac14,-\frac{\sqrt2}4,0\right)$.

lehigh-2003-33.title: Law of cosines twice
lehigh-2003-33.body:
Let $C$'s radius be $r$. Then $AB=8$, $AC=3+r$, $BC=5+r$. Law of cosines at $A$:
$$(r+5)^2=8^2+(r+3)^2-2\cdot8(r+3)\cdot\tfrac{11}{16}.$$
Expanding: $10r+25=73+6r-11r-33$, so $15r=15$ and $r=1$.

So $AC=4$, $BC=6$, $AB=8$. Law of cosines at $B$: $4^2=8^2+6^2-2\cdot8\cdot6\cos B$, so $\cos B=\frac{84}{96}=\frac78$.

**Answer: $\frac78$**

lehigh-2003-34.title: Powers of two differing by 6
lehigh-2003-34.body:
The factors $x-4$ and $x-10$ differ by $6$ and their product is a positive power of $2$ (so $y\ge0$), hence both are powers of $2$ or both are negatives of powers of $2$.

Powers of $2$ differing by $6$: $8$ and $2$. Negatives: $-2$ and $-8$. These give $x-4=8$ (so $x=12$) or $x-4=-2$ (so $x=2$), each with product $16=2^4$, so $y=4$.

Solutions $(12,4)$ and $(2,4)$: $2$ of them.

**Answer: 2**

lehigh-2003-35.title: Use the number of 20-packets
lehigh-2003-35.body:
Using only $6$s and $9$s one can make exactly the multiples of $3$ that are at least $6$ (and $0$). So $N$ is attainable iff for some $k\ge0$, $N-20k$ is $0$ or a multiple of $3$ that is at least $6$.

For $N=43$: $43,\ 23,\ 3$ for $k=0,1,2$ are not $0$ or multiples of $3$ that are at least $6$ ($43$ and $23$ are not multiples of $3$, $3$ is too small). So $43$ cannot be bought.

For $N\ge44$: $N-20k$ for $k=0,1,2$ have three different residues mod $3$ (since $20\equiv2$), so one of them is a multiple of $3$; it is at least $N-40\ge4$, hence at least $6$. So every $N\ge44$ can be bought.

**Answer: 43**

lehigh-2003-36.title: Coordinates
lehigh-2003-36.body:
Put $A=(-1,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,\sqrt3)$. The square on $AB$ is $[-1,1]\times[0,2]$. The inward unit normal of $AC$ is $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,-\frac12\right)$, so the square on $AC$ has its outer edge from $A+(\sqrt3,-1)$ to $C+(\sqrt3,-1)$, lying on the line $\sqrt3x-y=4-\sqrt3$. By symmetry the square on $BC$ has its outer edge on $-\sqrt3x-y=4-\sqrt3$.

The three squares fit into the equilateral triangle bounded by the line $y=2$ (the top of the square on $AB$) and these two lines. Those two lines meet at $E=(0,\sqrt3-4)$, so the altitude of this triangle is $2-(\sqrt3-4)=6-\sqrt3$ and its side is $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}(6-\sqrt3)=4\sqrt3-2$.

Checking all orientations of an equilateral triangle (side $=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\cdot$ sum of the three support heights, minimized numerically over rotations) confirms that this orientation is the smallest.

**Answer: $4\sqrt3-2$**

lehigh-2003-37.title: Pair subsets
lehigh-2003-37.body:
Pair each subset $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,5\}$ with $S\cup\{6\}$. In $S\cup\{6\}$ the number $6$ is largest (added) and every other element has its sign flipped relative to its sign in $S$. So the alternating sums of the two subsets add to $6$ (for $S=\varnothing$ the pair is just $\{6\}$, also $6$).

There are $2^5=32$ pairs, giving $6\cdot32=192$.

**Answer: 192**

lehigh-2003-38.title: Finite differences
lehigh-2003-38.body:
Let $g(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)$ and $h(x)=g(x+2)-g(x)$. The expression equals $g(x+6)-g(x+4)-g(x+2)+g(x)=h(x+4)-h(x)$.

If $p$ has leading term $Ax^n$, then $p(x+k)-p(x)$ has leading term $Ank\,x^{n-1}$. So $g$ has leading term $3x^2$, $h$ has leading term $12x$, and $h(x+4)-h(x)$ has leading term $48$ and degree $0$.

The polynomial is the constant $48$.

**Answer: 48**

lehigh-2003-39.title: Factor $f(f(x))$
lehigh-2003-39.body:
$f(f(x))=f(x)\big(f(x)+k\big)=f(x)\,(x^2+kx+k)$. The solution set of $f(f(x))=0$ is that of $f(x)=0$ plus the real roots of $x^2+kx+k=0$. We need those extra roots to be solutions of $f(x)=0$ (i.e. $x=0$ or $x=-k$) or to not exist.

If $x=0$ or $x=-k$ is a root of $x^2+kx+k$, then $k=0$, which works. Otherwise $x^2+kx+k=0$ has no real roots iff $k^2-4k<0$ iff $0<k<4$.

So the set is $0\le k<4$.

**Answer: $[0,4)$**

lehigh-2003-40.title: Isolate and square
lehigh-2003-40.body:
The right side is nonnegative, so $x>0$, and the radicands need $x\ge1$. Move one radical: $x-\sqrt{x-\frac1x}=\sqrt{1-\frac1x}$. Squaring:
$$x^2-2x\sqrt{x-\tfrac1x}+x-\tfrac1x=1-\tfrac1x\ \Longrightarrow\ x^2+x-1=2x\sqrt{x-\tfrac1x}=2\sqrt{x(x^2-1)}.$$
Write $x^2+x-1=(x^2-1)+x$. Then $(x^2-1)-2\sqrt{x(x^2-1)}+x=0$, i.e. $\left(\sqrt{x^2-1}-\sqrt x\right)^2=0$.

So $x^2-1=x$, and the positive root is $x=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.

Check: $x-\frac1x=1$ and $1-\frac1x=\frac1{x^2}$ (as $x^2=x+1$), so the right side is $1+\frac1x=x$. ✓

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$**
